text: The best ones are framed by a short cover note explaining what is inside and why.
The cover note is the only document investors read before forming a working opinion of how organized you are.
it has three short paragraphs: what you're raising and on what terms, what's inside the data room and where to start, and how to reach you with questions.
A cover note written first describes what you intend to include; a cover note written last describes what's actually there, which is the only version that holds up under diligence.
the gap between what the cover note promises and what the room contains is the first thing a careful investor will notice.
Keep it specific, keep it short, and avoid re-pitching the deck.

A Columbia Business School venture professor says founders put their four best numbers on the slide and an investor's job is to ask about the other metrics. She says a founder who cannot answer questions about the numbers left out is a signal to dig. TechCrunch reports her words; the reporter's article is the only record.

A TechCrunch report on a lawsuit by SoftBank against the events app IRL says an investigation found most of the app's users were fake. It is one of the cases behind the point that investors cannot skip checking traction at the earliest stages.

Prosecutors said the real figure was about one tenth of what was shown. Rare, but it is the case that turns a deck number into a crime.

Gust's founder wrote in 2012 that angels react largely on intuition and that faith in the entrepreneur is among the most important factors, which is why a 2 to 3 minute video helps when screening many submissions.

At a 2025 panel of Philadelphia-area investors, one said his last half-dozen deals were pitched in person rather than over Zoom or slides. Another suggested a 90-second pitch video for the firm's associate or analyst when the principal cannot meet yet. Reported by Technical.ly.

CNN reported that the engineering firm Arup lost about $25 million when an employee joined a video call in which the other participants were fake re-creations of colleagues. Police and the company confirmed fake voices and images were used. The case concerns a company, not an investor, but it shows that a convincing recorded or live video of a real person can be synthetic.
